newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs Roche hypertension drug.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs Roche hypertension drug.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory committee voted 5-3 Friday to recommend approval of Roche Holding Ltd's mibefradil (Posicor) for hypertension.
The panel also voted 5-3 to recommend the drug to be taken along with other common drugs for chronic stable angina, the chest pain that results from narrowing of coronary arteries.
The FDA does not have to follow the panel's advice, but usually does.

Mibefradil is a long-acting calcium channel blocker, a class of drugs that reduces the strength of heart muscle contractions. Short-acting versions have been plagued by recent reports that they may be worsening cardiac disease and contributing to premature deaths.
Mibefradil is a new generation and does not show evidence of these problems, said Robert Pordy, Roche director of international clinical research.

The FDA was concerned about changes seen in some patients' electrocardiogram measures. Panelists engaged Roche in a lengthy debate about whether there was a potential for adverse cardiac events due to these changes.
"It's hard to say there are no safety concerns at this point," said panel member Robert Califf of Duke University Medical Center, who voted against approval.

Panel member Lemuel Moye, who also voted against approval, said he felt that six deaths in 160 patients taking mibefradil in a pilot study in congestive heart failure indicated that "something strange is going on," and that he wanted more assurance that the drug was not contributing to lethal events.
Others said they felt reasonably assured that mibefradil was as safe as other commonly used drugs in the class.

The FDA did not question mibefradil's efficacy. Roche director of clinical research Isaac Kobrin presented data from four placebo-controlled trials in hypertension and five placebo-controlled trials in angina.

The data measured results in a total of 3,430 patients. Mibefradil normalized blood pressure in half the patients taking the initial 50 mg daily dose, and in 60-to-70 percent of patients taking the maintenance 100 mg dose.

In angina, the drug increased patients' exercise time on treadmill tests by 50 seconds -- a significant increase, according to Pordy. Thirty-eight percent of patients taking 100 mg had at least one side effect, with headache being the most common. Very few patients dropped out of the trials due to adverse events.

Analysts estimate that, if approved, mibefradil could have sales of 600 to 800 million swiss francs over the next five years. The drug is approved for hypertension and chronic stable angina in the Netherlands and Switzerland.
